result.summary: Ovid describes the decline of the world from the Silver Age under Jupiter, through the Brazen Age, to the Iron Age. In the Iron Age crime, greed, war and family betrayal spread, and the goddess Astræa leaves the Earth.

scenes.title: Silver and Brazen Ages
scenes.summary: Jupiter replaces Saturn, creates the seasons, and humans take to houses and farming. The Brazen Age follows, fiercer but not impious.
scenes.stakes: Humanity loses the easy perpetual spring and begins to suffer heat, cold and toil.

scenes.title: The Iron Age
scenes.summary: Crime, greed, seafaring, land division, mining and war arise; families turn on one another and Astræa abandons the Earth.
scenes.stakes: Justice, piety and human trust are lost, and the Earth is drenched in slaughter.

alias_notes.explanation: Ceres stands for grain, by metonymy.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable image of gold as more destructive than iron, summing up greed.
Astræa's departure marks the end of justice on Earth.

analysis.text: The passage presents history as moral decline, each age worse than the last, until justice leaves the world.
Ovid adapts Hesiod's myth of the Ages of Man, with a Roman focus on greed, seafaring and property.

legacy.text: The scheme of Golden, Silver, Brazen and Iron ages shaped later literature, and 'golden age' became a common phrase.

fun_facts.text: Hesiod listed five ages, including a Heroic one; Ovid's version has only four.

language_notes.text: Tartarus is the deepest part of the underworld, where Jupiter sent Saturn after overthrowing him. Jupiter is the Greek Zeus; Saturn the Greek Cronus.
Pendant means hanging, here describing icicles.
Seeds of Ceres means grain; Ceres was goddess of agriculture, so her name stands for the crop itself.
Stygian refers to the Styx, a river of the underworld; the passage means riches were hidden in the earth near the realm of the dead.
Wolfsbane is aconite, a deadly poison; stepmothers poisoning stepchildren was a common figure of Roman literature.

context_notes.text: Ovid presents four declining ages: Gold, Silver, Brass (bronze) and Iron, a scheme borrowed from the poet Hesiod.
Astræa was the goddess of justice, daughter of Jupiter's line of Titans; her departure marks the end of justice on earth. She later became the constellation Virgo.

literary_notes.text: Repeating 'Then, for the first time' across sentences 4 to 6 marks each new hardship as a fresh loss.
Ships are described as pine trees that once stood on mountains, now bounding over waves, suggesting nature violated and transformed by human ambition.
War is made a figure who brandishes bloody weapons, and gold is called worse than iron, a bitter judgment on greed.
Clipped lists of crimes and family betrayals pile up quickly, mirroring how moral collapse spreads without restraint.
